doc_summary: Greenblatt argues that evidence of AI misalignment from internals-based methods (ELK heads, interpretability, probes) alone is unlikely to convince decision-makers, so legible evidence must bottom out in behavior humans can understand. Internals methods remain useful for finding behavioral evidence, supporting interpretations of behavior, and being iterated against.

items.claim: Prefers evidence that bottoms out in human-understandable behavior over purely internals-based evidence (probes, ELK heads, interpretability) because the latter is unlikely to convince relevant people enough to trigger strong action.
items.quote: More generally, I think that to convince people enough to take strong action, evidence will need to bottom out in some sort of behavioral evidence that (many) humans can understand.

items.claim: Distrusts probe or interpretability signals (e.g. a deception probe firing more on fake escape opportunities) as standalone proof of misalignment, even if the method is theoretically and empirically well supported.
items.quote: This reasoning also applies to "our interpretability method decoded some very problematic deceptive reasoning" or "the deception probe fires in a very suspicious way (e.g. it fires more when we give it a fake opportunity to escape or ask it about its alignment research outputs)".

items.claim: Counts internals evidence as potentially sufficient when it is directly supported by behavior, such as reasoning that looks malign and is predictive of actions, with Alignment Faking cited as a good mix of CoT inspection and behavioral evidence.
items.quote: Internals-based evidence which is substantially behaviorally supported (in a relatively direct way) could suffice. E.g., if we can read off the AI's internal reasoning using some fancy method, it looks quite malign, and the malign aspects of the reasoning are also quite predictive of the AI's behavior, this could suffice.

items.claim: Distrusts behavioral evidence found under heavy optimization pressure, since with enough search any model can be made to look misaligned; the amount of optimization applied must be legibly limited.
items.quote: However, it will be important to legibly not apply too much optimization pressure as you might be able to get any model to look misaligned with enough optimization pressure.

items.claim: Prefers methods that find inputs on which the AI behaves egregiously badly in a way humans can understand over internals-only detection, because such inputs convert detection into legible behavioral evidence.
items.quote: The technique could allow us to find behavioral evidence that would have otherwise been hard to find. For instance, maybe we can use the method to discover an input on which the AI does something egregiously bad (that we can understand).

items.claim: Solid behavioral evidence is necessary but not necessarily sufficient to trigger a strong response, so claims about evidence should be hedged accordingly.
items.quote: (That's not to say solid behavioral evidence will necessarily suffice.)

items.claim: Prefers internals-based understanding as a supporting piece of evidence for interpreting observed behavior (e.g. sabotage) over a heavily load-bearing component, because it can back up or undercut a given interpretation but is unlikely to carry the case alone.
items.quote: However, for usage as legible evidence, this internals-based understanding is unlikely to work as a heavily load-bearing component, while it might work as a more minor/moderate piece of evidence in support of a given interpretation.

items.claim: Researchers should choose what to build by thinking through the ultimate use case (who must be convinced, what response is triggered) and altering their approach accordingly.
items.quote: I think researchers working on internals-based techniques for detecting misalignment should spend some time thinking about the ultimate use case of their technique and then alter their approach as needed.

items.claim: Detection that does not convince everyone can still be valuable, by giving partial buy-in, letting believers adjust control protocols, triggering preexisting commitments, or serving as a detector to iterate against.
items.quote: If we can detect misalignment, we can study techniques for preventing or removing misalignment by iterating (or even training) against our detectors. The more robust the detector is, the more useful this would be.

items.claim: Legible evidence has an upper bound: once even well-elicited debate cannot make a subtle or complex bad action understandable to humans, misaligned AIs can act without producing legible evidence.
items.quote: once well elicited debate (and other methods for improving human understanding) aren't viable, misaligned AIs can get away with doing bad actions without these actions resulting in legible evidence of misalignment.
